title: Subject pronouns
rule: io, tu, lui, lei, Lei, noi, voi, loro. The verb ending already shows the person, so the pronoun is used mainly for emphasis or contrast.

head: Pronoun
English
Notes
rows: lower-case, even at the start of a sentence it is just io
friends, family, children, people who offered it
capital L in writing; verb in the third person, like lui / lei
any group, formal or informal, in everyday Italian
rare: hotels, old-fashioned service. Recognise it, don't use it

items.t: Io sono di Toronto, lei è di Bari.
items.n: I am from Toronto, she is from Bari.

items.note: after anche (also) and neanche (not even) the pronoun is needed

blocks.title: egli, ella, esso, essa
blocks.text: Old grammar books list *egli* (he), *ella* (she), *esso / essa* (it) and *essi / esse* (they). You will meet them in literature and in formal writing; nobody says them. Spoken and modern written Italian use [[lui]], [[lei]], [[loro]].

blocks.title: There is no "it"
blocks.text: Italian has no subject pronoun for things. [[Il treno è in ritardo.|The train is late.]] and then simply [[È in ritardo.|It is late.]]: the verb alone carries "it".

items.wrong: Io sono Luca, io sono canadese, io sono di Toronto.
items.right: Sono Luca, sono canadese, sono di Toronto.
items.why: Dropping the pronoun is the default, not an option.
Capital L marks the formal you in writing.
No pronoun for things; the verb is enough.

items.q: «Siamo di Roccamarina.» Which pronoun is implied?
In everyday spoken Italian, a group of people is addressed as voi, whether formal or not.
items.why: Loro as a formal plural survives only in very formal service situations.
